topics.title: 1.1 Listening: What is a lecture? and effective note-taking

paragraphs: A lecture is an organized talk in which a lecturer presents information about a subject to students. Lectures are an important source of academic information, but students cannot be expected to remember everything they hear.
Note-taking is the selective recording of important information, not verbatim transcription.
sections.heading: Why note-taking matters
bullets: Record important information for later revision.
Prepare for assignments and examinations.
Identify main ideas and supporting details.
Review notes soon after a lecture to fill gaps while the information is fresh.

sections.heading: Before, during and after a lecture
bullets: Before: read about the subject, arrive early, prepare materials and listen to the introduction.
During: listen for main points, verbal and visual cues, topics and supporting details.
Use short phrases, keywords, abbreviations and symbols rather than complete sentences.
After: review immediately, add missing points, organize headings and clarify unclear abbreviations.

topics.title: 1.2 Grammar: Modals and infinitives for giving advice

sections.heading: Advice forms
paragraphs: Advice can be expressed using should, ought to, had better, or an imperative or infinitive form.

rows: You ought to read before class.
strong advice with an implied consequence

sections.heading: Important points
bullets: Use the base form after should: should study.
Use ought to: ought to study.
Use had better + base verb: had better go.
The negative form is should not or had better not.

sections.heading: Purposes and approaches
bullets: Reading for study: understand and remember important information.
Reading for pleasure/escapism: read mainly for enjoyment.
Reading instructions: read to perform a task.
Skimming: obtain the general idea or overview quickly.
Scanning: locate a particular piece of information quickly.
Detailed reading: understand ideas and supporting details carefully.

sections.heading: Good academic reading
bullets: Identify why you are reading.
Preview headings and the organization of the text.
Select an approach that matches the purpose.
Identify main ideas and supporting details.
Make notes in your own words.
Evaluate what the author communicates.
Review and use the information.

sections.heading: Form
paragraphs: The present perfect uses subject + have/has + past participle.
Examples: I have studied; He has studied; Have they studied?
bullets: An action at an unspecified time before now.
A past action with a present result.
An action that has recently stopped.
An experience that happened once, never or several times.
An action or situation that began in the past and continues to the present.

sections.heading: Present perfect and simple past
paragraphs: The present perfect focuses on experience or a result up to now and does not normally state a definite finished past time. The simple past describes a completed action at a definite time.
bullets: Common signals: already, ever, never, just, not yet, so far, up to now, till now.

rows: I have read this novel before.
I read it two years ago.

rows: If + present simple, will + base verb
If I meet her, I will ask a question.
If + past simple, would + base verb
If I met him, I would talk to him.
If + past perfect, would have + past participle
If I had studied, I would have passed.

sections.heading: Key points
bullets: The if-clause states the condition; the main clause states the result.
The clauses can change position.
Do not normally use will in the if-clause.
Provided (that), as long as and on condition that can introduce conditions.

sections.heading: Main ideas
bullets: Team sports are an effective way to exercise.
Regular practice and games help maintain a routine.
Team sports encourage healthy competition and sportsmanship.
Players should show respect whether they win or lose.
Team sports offer opportunities to make friends and learn about games and people.
Choices include action, ball, accuracy and water sports.

sections.heading: Reading skills
paragraphs: Sportsmanship means behaving fairly and respectfully toward other players and teams, whether winning or losing.
bullets: Find the main idea and supporting details.
Identify pronoun references.
Decide whether statements are true, false or not given.
Use evidence from the passage.

sections.heading: What context means
paragraphs: Context is the surrounding words, sentences and ideas that help readers understand an unfamiliar word.

sections.heading: How to guess meaning
bullets: Read the sentence containing the unfamiliar word.
Read the surrounding sentences.
Look for examples, explanations or contrasts.
Consider the word's grammatical role.
Substitute a possible meaning and check sense.
Confirm with a dictionary when available.

sections.heading: Cultural tourism
paragraphs: Cultural tourism involves travel motivated by interest in culture, traditions, heritage and ways of life.

sections.heading: Benefits and risks
bullets: Potential benefits include income, employment, markets for local products and appreciation of heritage.
Poor management may disrupt local customs, change practices for visitors, distribute benefits unfairly or pressure resources.

sections.heading: Responsible management
bullets: Involve local communities.
Respect local values and practices.
Protect cultural heritage.
Ensure benefits reach affected communities.

topics.title: 3.3 Strategies for improving English grammar knowledge

sections.heading: Practical strategies
bullets: Read extensively.
Notice grammar in English texts.
Write examples and repeat structures.
Reread writing to find and correct mistakes.
Review structures learned in class.
Use a grammar reference.
Complete exercises.

sections.heading: Effective learning cycle
paragraphs: Notice a structure, understand its form and use, study examples, create your own sentences, use it in speaking or writing, and review and correct mistakes.

sections.heading: Main facts
bullets: Awramba is in Fogera woreda, Debub Gondar Zone, about 73 kilometres east of Bahir Dar.
Zumra Nuru and 19 others founded it in 1980.
The community aimed to address socio-economic problems through mutual help and egalitarianism.
It promotes equal rights for women and men and no gender-based division of labour.
It values hard work, helping others, cleanliness and discipline.
Members faced social exclusion and difficulty obtaining fertile land.
Weaving and milling provide income.
The community provides education and social support.

sections.heading: Reading themes
bullets: Intentional community and shared goals
Egalitarianism and gender equality
Economic adaptation
Mutual support
Cultural difference and resilience

sections.heading: Positive and negative interaction
paragraphs: Positive interaction includes coexistence and situations where people and wildlife benefit or live without harmful conflict.
Negative interaction occurs when people and animals compete over resources or wildlife affects safety, crops or livelihoods.

sections.heading: Geography
paragraphs: The passage describes African rainforests extending from the west coast toward Kenya and Tanzania. More than 80 percent of the rainforest area discussed is in the Congo Basin. Madagascar is off Africa's southeast coast in the Indian Ocean.

sections.heading: Animals
bullets: Lemurs: found in Madagascar, endangered and vegetarian; examples include the indri and mouse lemur.
Mountain gorillas: live in Rwanda, DR Congo and Uganda in small groups led by a dominant male.
Forest elephants: live in the Congo Basin and are smaller than African elephants.
Chimpanzees: use twigs and stones or branches to obtain food.
Baboons: mentioned as other forest animals.

sections.heading: Meaning
bullets: Denotation is the literal or dictionary meaning.
Connotation is the feeling, association or emotional meaning.
A connotation may be positive, negative or neutral.

sections.heading: Example
paragraphs: Group, clique and club can refer to a set of people, but carry different associations. Clique can suggest a closed group that excludes others, while group is more neutral.

sections.heading: Examples
bullets: If tourists visit the park, they will see wildlife.
If I lived near the park, I would visit it.
If we had protected the habitat, fewer animals would have been affected.

sections.heading: Key terms
paragraphs: Population is the number of people living in a country or region.
Dense means crowded or closely packed.
Density describes how closely something is packed into a given space.
Population density is the number of people living in a unit of area.

sections.heading: Calculation
paragraphs: Population density = total population divided by land area.
It is commonly expressed as people per square kilometre.
The exact teacher-read listening script is not printed in the supplied PDF. Script-specific answers must not be invented.
sections.heading: Listening and interpretation
bullets: High density means many people live within a relatively small area.
Low density means relatively few people live within a larger area.
Density can vary with available population and area data.

sections.heading: How to read
paragraphs: A population pyramid, or age-sex pyramid, is a bar graph showing a population divided by age and sex.
bullets: The vertical axis shows age groups.
Each horizontal bar represents an age group.
The left side represents males and the right side females.
Percentages are read outward from the centre.
Add male and female percentages for an age group to obtain the total.

sections.heading: Planning and factors
bullets: Birth rates and death rates affect shape.
Age structure and sex ratio are important.
Migration affects population structure.
Interpret only the actual graph and its labels.

sections.heading: Definition
paragraphs: A collocation is a sequence or combination of words that commonly occur together in conventional usage.

sections.heading: Examples

middle management

sections.heading: Learning strategy
paragraphs: Record words together with the words they commonly accompany. Read and listen to authentic English, notice repeated combinations and learn phrases rather than isolated words.

sections.heading: Active and passive voice
paragraphs: Active voice: the subject performs the action. People developed a bar graph.
Passive voice: the subject receives or is affected by the action. A bar graph was developed.
The basic passive structure uses the correct form of be + past participle.

sections.heading: Changing active to passive
bullets: Move the active object to the subject position.
Choose the correct tense of be.
Use the past participle of the main verb.
Add by + agent only when the doer is important.

sections.heading: Changing passive to active
bullets: Identify the agent, if stated.
Make the agent the subject.
Use the correct tense.
Change the passive verb to its active form.
